item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=failure+modes+of+autonomous+agents+in+following+external+directives+when+safety+goals+conflict&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6572478\", \"title\": [\"Why AI Agents Fail: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Autonomous LLM-Based Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are no longer a research curiosity-they are being deployed in production environments across industries. Yet for all the progress in what these systems can do, comparatively little attention has been paid to how, and under what conditions, they break. This paper attempts to fill part of that gap. Drawing on over forty published works from 2020 through early 2025, I propose a four-dimensional taxonomy of LLM agent failure modes, organized around the core functional modules present in most agentic architectures: reasoning and planning, tool use and action execution, memory and context management, and multi-agent orchestration. For each dimension, I provide formal definitions of specific failure classes, describe triggering conditions, and supply concrete illustrative examples grounded in the empirical literature. I also introduce the Agent Robustness Evaluation Protocol (AREP)-a lightweight, framework-agnostic robustness evaluation methodology intended to surface latent failure risks before deployment rather than after. The paper concludes with seven practitioner recommendations for building agentic systems that are not merely capable, but meaningfully robust and reliable.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6572478\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"title\": [\"When Agentic AI Breaks Software Quality Assurance: Failure Modes, Reliability Risks, and Governance Strategies for Autonomous Testing Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing software quality assurance from a predominantly human-directed activity into an increasingly autonomous process in which AI systems can generate tests, execute programs, interpret failures, modify test suites, and iteratively refine their actions.
